title: Switzerland's direct democracy asks citizens to vote several times a year on complex legal, social and financial issues. For each national vote, the federal government publishes an official
voting booklet (Abstimmungsbüchlein)
b

explaining the proposal, its background, the arguments of supporters and opponents, and the position of the Federal Council and Parliament. These materials are a rich source of complex, structured and unstructured information — proposal descriptions, legal and financial detail, arguments, qualifications, dates, numbers and statements across different linguistic contexts — and an authoritative, relatively balanced basis for understanding what's being voted on. They therefore make a valuable
real-world document corpus for investigating how well multilingual models like Apertus understand and reason over complex documents.
b
During campaigns, voters meet many claims about proposals, and checking them against the official materials is difficult and time-consuming. This challenge explores how Apertus can be applied to this
document-grounded claim-verification
b
task, while remaining multilingual.

The solution should: correctly classify document–claim pairs (entailment/contradiction/neutral); provide the relevant evidence passage(s); support the benchmark languages; use Apertus as the primary model; be reproducible; and document how document context is prepared and supplied. A human-generated benchmark is provided during the challenge for development and testing.

title: What am I building, in one sentence?
b
An Apertus-powered application that decides whether a natural-language claim is entailed, contradicted, or unaddressed by an official Swiss voting booklet — and shows the supporting passage(s).

i.c: What am I building, in one sentence?
An Apertus-powered application that decides whether a natural-language claim is entailed, contradicted, or unaddressed by an official Swiss voting booklet — and shows the supporting passage(s).

title: What exactly is the task?
b
Document-grounded Natural Language Inference (NLI): Document + Claim → Entailment / Contradiction / Neutral. It's not general QA and not about real-world truth — only the claim–document relationship.

i.c: Document-grounded Natural Language Inference (NLI): Document + Claim → Entailment / Contradiction / Neutral. It's not general QA and not about real-world truth — only the claim–document relationship.

title: Which languages must it handle?
b
German, French and Italian, including cross-lingual pairs (booklet and claim may be in different languages).

i.c: German, French and Italian, including cross-lingual pairs (booklet and claim may be in different languages).

title: What data do I get?
b
Official voting booklets as PDFs, plus a benchmark of human-annotated document–claim pairs with supporting paragraphs. SNLI is an English reference set for familiarisation.

i.c: Official voting booklets as PDFs, plus a benchmark of human-annotated document–claim pairs with supporting paragraphs. SNLI is an English reference set for familiarisation.

title: Which model should I use?
b
Apertus, as the primary model. The document-processing approach (RAG, Docling, OCR, compression…) is open — a key comparison is full-document vs. retrieved/selected context.

i.c: Apertus, as the primary model. The document-processing approach (RAG, Docling, OCR, compression…) is open — a key comparison is full-document vs. retrieved/selected context.

title: How is it judged?
b
Macro-F1 over the three NLI classes on a held-out benchmark, plus evidence relevance, and efficiency (token usage and inference time).

i.c: Macro-F1 over the three NLI classes on a held-out benchmark, plus evidence relevance, and efficiency (token usage and inference time).
